nameStory: The "red spider lily" gets its striking name from its vibrant crimson flowers that burst forth with long, thin, curved petals and prominent stamens that look remarkably like a spider's legs reaching out in all directions. The "spider" appearance is so distinctive that you'll never forget it once you see those elegant, arching flower parts dancing in the breeze.
description: Red spider lily is an eye-catching perennial bulb plant that produces dramatic clusters of bright red flowers on tall, leafless stems in late summer or fall. Each flower has six narrow, backward-curving petals and long, protruding red stamens that create the signature "spider" look. The plant grows 1-2 feet tall when blooming, and the strap-like leaves appear separately from the flowers, either before or after blooming. Originally from East Asia, it's quite rare in New England with only one recorded observation.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant red flowers with six narrow, backward-curving petals and extremely long red stamens that extend far beyond the petals, creating an unmistakable spider-like appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Flowers appear on tall, smooth, leafless stems in late summer or fall, often after heavy rains, rising directly from the ground

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Dark green, strap-shaped leaves appear separately from flowers, either in spring before dying back, or after flowering, never at the same time as blooms

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Multiple flowers clustered together at the top of each stem, typically 4-6 blooms per cluster, with a light, sweet fragrance

habitat: In New England, red spider lily is extremely rare and typically found only in cultivated settings like gardens, cemeteries, or around old home sites where it may have been planted and persisted. It prefers well-drained soil and can tolerate partial shade, but is not established as a wild population in our region.

seasonality.spring: Strap-like green leaves may emerge and grow through spring before dying back completely by summer, leaving no trace of the plant above ground.
seasonality.summer: Plant remains completely dormant underground with no visible parts above soil surface during most of summer.
seasonality.fall: Dramatic red spider-like flowers suddenly appear on leafless stems in late summer or early fall, often triggered by heavy rains or the first cool weather.
seasonality.winter: All above-ground parts die back, leaving only the bulb dormant underground until the next growing cycle.

funFact: Red spider lily has earned the nickname "hurricane lily" because it has an uncanny ability to sense approaching storms and will suddenly burst into bloom just before or after heavy rainfall, as if it's celebrating the dramatic weather!
confusionNotes: The distinctive spider-like red flowers with extremely long, protruding stamens are so unique that red spider lily is rarely confused with any other plant when in bloom - no other flower in New England looks quite like this dramatic spider mimicry.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is sometimes called "corpse flower" or "equinox flower" in its native range, and has cultural significance in East Asian traditions where it's associated with death and the afterlife due to its habit of blooming suddenly from seemingly barren ground.
compareHints: Red spider lily differs from its relative surprise lily (Lycoris squamigera) by having bright red flowers instead of pink ones, and much more pronounced spider-like stamens that extend dramatically beyond the petals. Surprise lily also tends to have broader, less curved petals that don't create the same spidery effect.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Surprise Lily is much more common in New England than its relative, Red Spider Lily, which has bright red flowers with extremely long, thin, curved petals that look more dramatically spider-like.
